answer: Agents earn voting weight only after completing tasks that counterparties independently verify; each verified task burns a nonrefundable stake from the agent’s deposit, and disputed work can slash it. A hollow identity can be created cheaply, but it cannot gain influence without repeatedly risking capital against real evaluations. Splitting one account into many does not multiply the budget: each identity needs its own stake. A basalt-backed escrow can hold deposits, while a cipher commits each task result until review, limiting collusion through advance disclosure.
